subtype: Living with a very direct sibling [Receiver]
passage:
Monday. Pankaj came down in his new shirt for the school photo. His elder brother Suraj looked up from his toast. "That colour makes you look ill." Pankaj changed shirts and said nothing all the way to school.
Wednesday. Pankaj showed Suraj his science model. "The wiring's messy. It'll short." Pankaj snatched it back and slammed his door.
Friday. The model had shorted in class, just as Suraj said. That evening Pankaj knocked on his brother's door. "You were right about the wiring. But when you say things like that, it sounds like you think I'm useless." Suraj stared. "I didn't mean it that way." "I know. Can you just tell me what's wrong and how to fix it, and skip the 'ill' part?" Suraj nodded slowly, then pulled out a screwdriver.

qa.q: What did Suraj say about Pankaj's shirt colour?
qa.a: "That colour makes you look ill."

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel after the shirt comment, and how can you tell?
qa.a: He felt hurt and criticised; he changed shirts and said nothing all the way to school.

qa.q: What choice did Pankaj make on Friday, and what came of it?
qa.a: He told Suraj how the words landed and asked for the fix without the harsh part; Suraj nodded and got a screwdriver.

qa.q: How might Suraj have felt when Pankaj said his words sound like "you think I'm useless"?
qa.a: He seems surprised, since he meant no harm, and may realise his honesty was landing as an attack.

grounding: A teenager hurt by his brother's blunt remarks tells him how the words land and asks for the honest content without the harsh tone.

subtype: Living with a very direct sibling [Receiver]
passage: Francis, come and sit by your Aparna aunty. You're sulking because your sister called your haircut a disaster? Let me tell you about my sister Leela. When I was fourteen, she told me my singing was flat, my handwriting looked like ants, and my best friend was using me. Every one of those stung. For a year I thought she hated me. Then one day, after she said my essay was "boring in the middle", I told her, "Leela, when you say it like that, I hear that I'm boring." She was shocked. She said she only meant the middle paragraph. We made a rule: she says the true part, I ask for the useful part. The essay won a prize. And my friend was using me, by the way. So, what exactly did she say about the haircut?

qa.q: What did Leela say Aparna's handwriting looked like?
qa.a: She said it looked like ants.

qa.q: What did young Aparna believe about Leela for a year, and why?
qa.a: She thought Leela hated her, because every blunt remark stung.

qa.q: What turning point changed how the sisters spoke to each other?
qa.a: Aparna told Leela how "boring in the middle" landed, and they made a rule: Leela says the true part, Aparna asks for the useful part.

qa.q: How might Leela have felt hearing Aparna say "I hear that I'm boring"?
qa.a: She was shocked, since she only meant one paragraph, and may have realised her honesty was landing as an insult.

grounding: An aunt recalls being stung by a blunt older sister, telling her how the words landed, and learning to keep the honest part and drop the sting.

subtype: Living with a very direct sibling [Receiver]
passage: You know my brother Ramesh, right? Everyone thinks he's funny. Living with him is different. I'm Kiran, by the way, the one he calls 'the slow one'. Last week I showed him my science fair poster, and he said, 'Title's boring and the graph's upside down.' Just like that, mouth full of upma. I went to my room and didn't come out for dinner. Then I looked at the poster again. The graph was upside down. That was the worst part. So the next morning I told him, 'When you say it like that, all I hear is that I'm useless. I don't even hear the useful bit.' He actually stopped chewing. He said, 'I didn't mean useless. I meant fix the graph.' Now I do this thing in my head: what's the fact, and what's just his voice? The graph was the fact. The voice was just Ramesh.

qa.q: What did Ramesh say about the poster?
qa.a: 'Title's boring and the graph's upside down.'

qa.q: How did Kiran feel after Ramesh's comment on the poster?
qa.a: Kiran felt criticised and hurt, going off to the bedroom and skipping dinner.

qa.q: What habit is Kiran building, and why does it help?
qa.a: Asking 'what's the fact, and what's just his voice?', which lets Kiran use the useful part, fixing the graph, without hearing 'useless'.

qa.q: How might Ramesh have felt when Kiran told him how his words landed?
qa.a: Ramesh seemed surprised, stopping mid-chew, since he only meant 'fix the graph', not that Kiran was useless.

grounding: Shows a teenager hurt by a sibling's blunt remarks who tells him how they land and learns to separate the honest point from the tone.

subtype: Living with a very direct sibling [Receiver]
passage:
Monday. Jyoti hung her new painting of the lake over her desk. Her sister Rajni glanced in. 'Looks like a kid did it. The water's the wrong blue.' Jyoti took it down and stuffed it in the cupboard.
Wednesday. At dinner Jyoti finally said it. 'When you say things like that, it sounds like you think I'm hopeless.' Rajni frowned. 'I just said the blue was wrong.' 'You also said a kid did it. That's the part I heard.' Rajni was quiet for a while. 'Okay. That part was extra.'
Saturday. Jyoti took her debate speech to Rajni's room. 'Tell me honestly. Just the useful bits.' Rajni read it. 'Opening's strong. The middle drags.' Jyoti crossed out half a page, and felt fine.

qa.q: What did Rajni say was wrong with the painting?
qa.a: The water's the wrong blue.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling when she stuffed the painting in the cupboard?
qa.a: She felt hurt and criticised, as if Rajni thought she was hopeless.

qa.q: What did Jyoti do on Saturday that worked?
qa.a: She asked Rajni for honest, useful feedback only, so she could take the content, that the middle drags, without the sting.

qa.q: How might Rajni have seen her own comments before Wednesday?
qa.a: Rajni thought she was simply stating facts, like the wrong blue, and didn't notice the extra hurtful part.

grounding: Shows a teenager hurt by a direct sibling's remarks who tells her how they land and then asks for the honest content without the sting.

subtype: Living with a very direct sibling [Receiver]
passage: Uday, you think your sister is harsh? Let me tell you about my brother Prakash. When your Vasudha Ajji was fifteen, in our house in Mysuru, Prakash would look at my rangoli and say, 'Crooked. Start again.' At my singing: 'Flat on the third line.' I cried in the bathroom more times than I can count. I thought he hated me. One Deepavali, after he called my rangoli crooked in front of the neighbours, I went up to the terrace where he was flying his kite and said, 'When you say it like that, I hear that I'm no good. Is that what you mean?' He was so shocked he let go of the string. 'No! I mean the left side is crooked. The rest is the best on the street.' After that I always asked him, 'What's the fact?', and I stopped hearing the rest.

qa.q: What did Prakash say about Vasudha's singing?
qa.a: 'Flat on the third line.'

qa.q: What did young Vasudha believe about Prakash, and how did it feel?
qa.a: She thought he hated her, and felt so hurt that she cried in the bathroom many times.

qa.q: What turning point changed how Vasudha heard Prakash?
qa.a: Going up to the terrace and telling him how his words landed; he explained he meant only the left side, and she learned to ask 'What's the fact?'

qa.q: How might Prakash have felt on the terrace when Vasudha spoke?
qa.a: Prakash was shocked, letting go of his kite string, because he had never meant that she was no good.

grounding: Shows, in an elder's memory, a teenager hurt by a blunt brother who tells him how his words land and learns to separate the fact from the tone.

subtype: Living with a very direct sibling [Receiver]
passage:
The power went out at nine, the night before the school council speeches, so Mahima practised by candlelight in the room she shared with her older sister. Zainab listened from the top bunk, then said, "The middle part is boring. And you say 'basically' about eleven times."
Mahima's face went hot. She blew out the candle a little too hard. "Wow. Thanks."
"What? You asked."
In the dark, Mahima counted her breaths. Then she said, "When you say it like that, it sounds like the whole speech is bad. Is it?"
Zainab was quiet for a moment. "No. The opening is really good. I just meant the middle drags."
"Then say that part too, okay? It helps me hear the rest."
Mahima relit the candle, crossed out the extra 'basically's and cut the middle paragraph in half. Zainab climbed down to hold the page steady.

qa.q: Why was Mahima practising by candlelight?
qa.a: The power went out at nine, the night before the school council speeches.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling when Zainab called the middle part boring, and how can you tell?
qa.a: She felt stung and hurt: her face went hot, she blew out the candle a little too hard and said a flat "Wow. Thanks."

qa.q: Which step helped Mahima most, and why?
qa.a: She told Zainab how the words sounded and asked if the whole speech was bad. That let her keep the useful points about the middle and the 'basically's without carrying the sting.

qa.q: How does Zainab see her own comment?
qa.a: Zainab thought she was just being honest because Mahima asked. Once she heard how it landed, she said the opening was good and came down to help.

grounding: Shows a teen hurt by her sister's blunt feedback telling her how the words land and pulling the honest point apart from the tone.
